history.heading: Early Britain
paragraphs: Britain has been inhabited for hundreds of thousands of years; Stonehenge was built around 3000–2000 BCE. Celtic peoples lived there when the Romans conquered much of Britain from 43 CE, building Hadrian's Wall in the north. After Rome left around 410, Anglo-Saxons settled England, while Celtic kingdoms persisted in Wales, Scotland and Cornwall. Vikings raided and settled from the late 8th century.
In 1066 William of Normandy conquered England at the Battle of Hastings. Magna Carta (1215) limited royal power and became a symbol of liberty, and Parliament developed in the 13th century.

history.heading: Union and empire
paragraphs: England conquered Wales in the 13th century. Henry VIII broke with the Catholic Church in the 1530s, creating the Church of England, and the Elizabethan era saw Shakespeare and growing naval power. The English Civil War (1642–1651) led to the execution of Charles I, and the Glorious Revolution of 1688 established parliamentary supremacy. England and Scotland united as Great Britain in 1707, and Ireland joined in 1801.

Britain led the Industrial Revolution from the late 18th century and built the largest empire in history, covering about a quarter of the world's land by 1920. It was also deeply involved in the Atlantic slave trade, which it abolished in 1807, and slavery in 1833.

history.heading: The 20th century
paragraphs: Most of Ireland became independent in 1922, while Northern Ireland remained part of the United Kingdom. Britain fought in both world wars; in 1940, under Winston Churchill, it held out against Nazi Germany. After 1945 it created the National Health Service and welfare state, and most of its colonies became independent, many joining the Commonwealth.

The UK joined the European Economic Community in 1973. The Troubles in Northern Ireland ended with the 1998 Good Friday Agreement. Scotland and Wales gained devolved parliaments in 1999. In a 2014 referendum Scotland voted to remain in the UK. Queen Elizabeth II reigned from 1952 to 2022 and was succeeded by Charles III.

history.heading: Brexit
paragraphs: In a 2016 referendum, 52 percent voted to leave the European Union, and the UK left on 31 January 2020. The process caused years of political turmoil. In 2024 the Labour Party under Keir Starmer won a large majority, ending 14 years of Conservative government.

culture.heading: Four nations
paragraphs: The UK consists of England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, each with its own identity. English is the main language, and Welsh, Scottish Gaelic, Scots and Irish are also spoken. Christianity is the largest religion, and the UK is highly diverse, with large communities of South Asian, African, Caribbean and other origins.

British literature includes Chaucer, Shakespeare, Austen, Dickens, the Brontës, Orwell and J. K. Rowling. British music has had huge global influence, from the Beatles and Rolling Stones to Queen, Adele and Ed Sheeran.

culture.heading: Sport and traditions
paragraphs: The British invented or codified football, rugby, cricket, tennis and golf; the Premier League is the world's most watched football league, and Wimbledon is the most famous tennis tournament. Traditions include afternoon tea, the pub, fish and chips, and royal ceremonies such as the Changing of the Guard.

politics.heading: Parliamentary monarchy
paragraphs: The UK is a constitutional monarchy and parliamentary democracy without a single written constitution. The prime minister leads the government, responsible to the elected House of Commons; the House of Lords is unelected. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have devolved governments.

The UK is a permanent member of the UN Security Council, a nuclear power, a founding member of NATO and a member of the G7. It remains a key supporter of Ukraine and maintains close ties with the United States.

economy.heading: A services economy
paragraphs: The UK has one of the world's largest economies, dominated by services. London is one of the world's top financial centres. Other strengths include professional services, education, research, pharmaceuticals (AstraZeneca, GSK), aerospace (Rolls-Royce, BAE Systems), creative industries, and North Sea oil and gas.

The currency is the pound sterling. Challenges include low productivity growth, trade friction with the EU after Brexit, regional inequality, high living costs and pressure on public services such as the NHS.
